title: Supervision 8 revision essays
description: Five more essay titles on this week’s lectures. Write one for practice, and hand it in if you’d like feedback on it.
instructions:
Optional, for revision. These essay titles go with this week’s lectures. Only the Supervision 8 essay has to be handed in.

  • Choose one and write it here, as you would in the exam. Leave the others blank: you can still submit.
  • Handing in. If you’d like my feedback on it, hand it in once you’ve submitted, in the same way as the work for this week. It goes into the same folder in my Google Drive.
  • Planning an answer to each of the others (your argument, your evidence and the order you’d put them in) is good revision too.
  • After you submit, Review my answers shows you the ground each title covers.
  • Pasting. As in the exam, you can copy and paste within your work, but you can’t paste in text copied from anywhere else. Write everything in your own words.

questions.title: Regulating the pH of the blood
questions.text: By what mechanisms is the pH of the blood regulated?
questions.guidance:
Here are some points to consider. It isn’t a model answer.

  • Buffers: the bicarbonate system (an open system: physiological buffering), phosphate, plasma proteins, haemoglobin (with the Haldane effect, in CO2 transport), and intracellular proteins in the longer term.
  • The lungs: chemoreceptors, central and peripheral; the control of PCO2; respiratory compensation.
  • The kidneys: reabsorbing filtered HCO3−; making new HCO3− from glutamine; titratable acid; HCO3− secretion in alkalosis; what regulates H+ secretion (plasma HCO3− and pH, PCO2, the filtered load, K+, ECF volume, angiotensin II and aldosterone).
  • The liver: urea or glutamine. And how they work together over seconds, minutes and days.

questions.title: Acidosis
questions.text: How may acidosis arise? How is it compensated for?
questions.guidance:
Here are some points to consider. It isn’t a model answer.

  • Respiratory acidosis: hypoventilation (lung disease, weak respiratory muscles, opioids and other drugs that depress the respiratory centre), so PCO2 rises; it can develop fast, so the uncompensated state is seen. Renal and hepatic compensation over days: more H+ secretion (CO2 acidifies the tubule cells) and more new HCO3−; the lecture’s example: pH 7.30, HCO3− 40 mM, PCO2 80 mmHg.
  • Metabolic acidosis: ketoacidosis (insulin lack; acetoacetic and β-hydroxybutyric acids), lactic acidosis (heavy exercise, shock), renal failure, loss of HCO3− (diarrhoea), hyperkalaemia. Respiratory compensation develops with it (the PCO2 falls about 1.2 mmHg per mM fall in HCO3−; deep, rapid Kussmaul breathing), then renal correction with the liver’s glutamine.
  • The consequences: K+ leaves cells (hyperkalaemia); effects on the heart, on enzymes and on haemoglobin’s affinity for O2 (the Bohr effect).
  • A pH–bicarbonate diagram makes a good figure for this title.

questions.title: Cells and the ECF
questions.text: Discuss the mechanisms that regulate cellular and extracellular pH.
questions.guidance:
Here are some points to consider. It isn’t a model answer.

  • Intracellular pH (about 7.1–7.2): intracellular buffers (proteins, phosphates); membrane transporters that extrude acid (the Na+/H+ exchanger, Na+-coupled HCO3− transport) and load it (Cl−/HCO3− exchange); CO2 crosses membranes easily, H+ doesn’t.
  • Extracellular pH: buffers, the lungs and the kidneys, as in the other titles.
  • Links between them: tubule cells sense their own pH, and it sets their H+ secretion; K+ and H+ exchange across cell membranes (hypokalaemia acidifies cells and causes a metabolic alkalosis); the central chemoreceptors sense the pH of the brain’s interstitial fluid; intracellular proteins buffer extracellular acid in the long term.
  • A special case: the red cell, with carbonic anhydrase and the chloride shift, carries CO2 and buffers H+ with haemoglobin.

questions.title: The kidney and acid–base balance
questions.text: Discuss the role of the kidney in acid–base balance, contrasting the functions of the proximal and distal parts of the nephron.
questions.guidance:
Here are some points to consider. It isn’t a model answer.

  • Proximal tubule: most of the filtered HCO3− (about 85%) is reabsorbed, by secondary active H+ secretion (NHE3) with luminal and cellular carbonic anhydrase, and NBC1 at the basolateral membrane; a large flux, but a small gradient (it can’t make the fluid very acid); glutamine catabolism makes NH4+ and new HCO3−.
  • The loop of Henle: 10–15% of filtered HCO3−; NH4+ reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb (on NKCC2 and K+ channels, and paracellularly), building up NH4+ in the medulla.
  • Distal tubule and collecting duct: type A intercalated cells secrete H+ by primary active transport (the H+-ATPase and the H+/K+-ATPase): a small flux, but a steep gradient, down to a urine pH of about 4.5; titratable acid; NH3 secreted and trapped as NH4+; type B cells secrete HCO3− in alkalosis.
  • The contrast: bulk and fixed against fine and regulated, as for Na+; leaky against tight epithelia; how each is regulated (pH, PCO2, K+, angiotensin II, aldosterone).

questions.title: pH in the fluid compartments
questions.text: How is the pH in the various extracellular fluid compartments regulated? Illustrate your answer with reference to one named example of an acidosis and one named example of an alkalosis.
questions.guidance:
Here are some points to consider. It isn’t a model answer.

  • The compartments: plasma, interstitial fluid and the CSF, which has little protein and so little non-bicarbonate buffer, and is separated from the blood by the blood–brain barrier, which CO2 crosses easily but HCO3− doesn’t; that’s why the central chemoreceptors respond so quickly to PCO2.
  • The mechanisms: buffers, the lungs and the kidneys, and the liver; transport of HCO3− into and out of the CSF over hours to days.
  • An acidosis: diabetic ketoacidosis, say, from its cause through respiratory compensation to renal correction; or a respiratory acidosis in lung disease.
  • An alkalosis: altitude (respiratory, compensated by the kidneys, and the CSF’s HCO3− adjusts too, which lets ventilation rise further); or vomiting (metabolic: gastric H+ lost while its HCO3− goes into the blood; hypoventilation; volume and K+ depletion keep it going).
